title: On the Slow Convergence to Trivial Solutions of Algorithms for Hard Optimization Problems
authors: Ali Hussaini Umar, Jean Barbier, Matthieu Jonckheere, Manuel Sáenz
abstract: Hard combinatorial optimization problems, many of which are NP-hard, present fundamental algorithmic challenges. Average-case analysis on random instances has emerged as a powerful framework for understanding typical algorithmic performance beyond worst-case guarantees. A substantial body of work has established negative results: for sufficiently hard instances (often controlled by the underlying graph connectivity/constraints density), no known polynomial-time algorithm can significantly outperform naive heuristics in the double asymptotic limit where both problem size and constraints density tend to infinity. We revisit this picture by studying the finite-size behavior of some optimization algorithms across easy, intermediate, and hard regimes. Through rigorous analysis of large-graph asymptotics combined with numerical experiments on canonical problems (maximum independent set and maximum $K$-SAT), we demonstrate that while algorithms do eventually converge to theoretically predicted bounds, this convergence can be remarkably slow. In the intermediate regime where instances are already highly constrained, local algorithms achieve solutions substantially better than their predicted performance in the high-constraint-density limit. This gap between finite-regime and asymptotic behavior has important practical implications: sophisticated algorithmic design remains crucial even when asymptotic theory predicts inevitable failure.
summary: This paper analyzes how well algorithms perform on hard optimization problems like MIS and Max K-SAT, moving beyond worst-case asymptotic guarantees. It demonstrates that even when theory predicts failure in the limit, sophisticated algorithms can achieve surprisingly good results in finite, intermediate regimes. This highlights the continued practical importance of algorithmic design even when asymptotic theory suggests otherwise.
main_problem: The paper investigates the algorithmic performance of solving hard, NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, such as Maximum Independent Set (MIS) and Max K-SAT.
main_result: While asymptotic theory predicts that no polynomial-time algorithm significantly outperforms heuristics in the limit, the study shows that convergence to these bounds can be remarkably slow, especially in the intermediate constraint regime.
method: The analysis combines rigorous average-case asymptotic analysis (using density evolution and population dynamics) with the study of finite-size behavior of various local and greedy algorithms.
model_or_system: The primary models are random graphs, specifically sparse Erdős-Rényi graphs $G(n, \lambda/n)$ and graphs derived from the configuration model, used to represent the constraints of the optimization problems.
key_observables: Performance ratios (e.g., $\sigma_A(G) / \sigma(G)$) comparing the algorithm's output size to the true maximum value ($\sigma(G)$).
important_parameters: Graph size ($n$), mean degree ($\lambda$), and the constraint density regime (easy, intermediate, hard).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on asymptotic limits ($n 	o \infty$) and approximations like Population Dynamics for message-passing algorithms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the average performance ratio of different algorithms (DG, SDG, MP) versus the mean degree $\lambda$. Figure 2 quantifies the convergence rate of the SDG algorithm towards a theoretical threshold.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the negative results in the double asymptotic limit. It then revisits the problem by analyzing finite-size behavior, applying techniques like density evolution and population dynamics to MIS and Max K-SAT to demonstrate slow convergence in intermediate regimes.
why_interesting: The study of algorithmic performance on highly constrained random systems, particularly the gap between finite-size and asymptotic behavior, is highly relevant to understanding the complexity of optimization problems encountered in quantum simulation and machine learning models.

Figure 2: Convergence of the performance ratio of static degree greedy (SDG) towards the half-bound threshold. The plot displays RSDG(λ) given by (11), interpreted as a natural performance lower bound for a large class of non-trivial algorithms for MIS, on Erdős-Rényi graphs G(n, λ/n) as a function of the degree λ in the limit of large n. The blue solid line represents the convergence of the theoretical results of SDG, while the red dashed line represents a power law fit for large values of λ.

Figure 3: Heatmap of the performance ratios of the degree greedy (DG) and static degree greedy (SDG) algorithms on Erdős-Rényi graphs G(n, λ/n). The left panel presents the results for DG, while the right panel shows the results for SDG. Both greedy algorithms achieve high ratios (above 1/2) for sparser graphs, but the ratios fall below 1/2 for denser graphs.
